verses.translation_literal: To the choirmaster, upon the Nehiloth: a psalm of David.
verses.translation_dramatic: For the choirmaster, to be sung to the Nehiloth: a psalm of David.
verses.directors_commentary:
Read this line as the label on a score, not as part of the prayer. The Hebrew verse count includes it as verse 1, which is why the KJV's numbers run one behind for the whole psalm: the KJV leaves it as an unnumbered heading.

The KJV's "upon Nehiloth" is honest in one way: it does not translate the word, because no one is sure what it means. The sources in front of us split. Rashi, following Menahem, takes it as the name of an instrument or a tune that the psalm is fitted to. Rashi also records an aggadic reading that links it to nachalah, "inheritance", and rejects it: that is not what the word means, and the psalm is not about inheritance. His own alternative is "swarms", as in a swarm of bees (b. Bava Kamma), and so a prayer against the hosts of enemies. Meiri, who admits that we do not know what these musical names mean, suggests an instrument whose notes come close and quick, like a swarm. Radak, quoting Rav Hai, hears the sound of bees hissing, and Metzudat Zion makes it a stringed or wind instrument with that sound. STEPBible's "flutes" is a guess of the same family. Do not play it as anything more than an unexplained stage direction.

The preposition "upon" is the same אֶל that Ibn Ezra says means עַל ("upon") here.

philological_notes.note: A musical direction of unknown meaning, found only here. Rashi, following Menahem, takes it as the name of an instrument; he records the aggadic reading 'inheritance' (nachalah) and rejects it as not the word's meaning; he proposes 'swarms' (gedudim, as a swarm of bees) as a better fit. Radak (after Rav Hai) and Metzudat Zion link it to the hiss of bees; Meiri to quick, close notes; Ibn Ezra thinks it may be the first words of a song. Left untranslated.

Participle of the Piel of נצח, 'the one who leads / is in charge', here the Temple music director. The same title opens many psalms. 'To the choirmaster' is the long-standing English rendering; the sense is a liturgical overseer, not a conductor in the modern sense.

verses.translation_literal: My words give ear to, YHWH; understand my sighing.
verses.translation_dramatic: Hear my words, LORD, and turn your ear to them. And where words fail me, let the low murmur of my heart be understood.
verses.directors_commentary: The psalm opens with two commands piled on each other, the speaker's voice taking the stance of a petitioner at a royal court. Notice the bodily image: ha'azinah is 'give ear', from ozen, ear, so the speaker asks God to cock his ear toward him. The second request goes deeper than speech. Hagigi is not 'meditation' in the cool, scholarly sense of the KJV; it is the inarticulate sound of a person who is muttering, sighing, groaning to himself. Rashi hears a speaker too burdened to find words, and Radak sets the two halves side by side: what I bring out of my mouth, hear; what I only mutter in my heart, understand. The KJV's 'consider my meditation' makes the speaker sound like a seminar student. In the ancient world, a request to a king began with getting his attention, and this is exactly that.

philological_notes.note: From the root for murmuring or muttering; here the unspoken sigh of the heart, set against the spoken 'words'. 'Meditation' (KJV) is too intellectual.
Here a command ('understand!'), not the noun 'understanding'. Rashi points out that the accent falls on the first syllable because this is the verb.

verses.translation_literal: Pay attention to the sound of my cry for help, my king and my God, for to you I pray.
verses.translation_dramatic: Listen to the sound of my crying out, my King and my God. For you are the one to whom I pray, and no one else.
verses.directors_commentary: Now the speaker names the relationship that licenses his plea: 'my King and my God'. In a world where a petitioner could only reach the king through the one who had power to decide his case, to call God 'my king' is to claim the right of a subject to be heard, and Radak says exactly this: I cry out to you as people cry to the king. The word shav'i is the cry of someone in trouble who needs rescue, not a polite request; Malbim notes that it is a cry for salvation (yeshuah). The final clause, ki elekha etpallal, puts the 'to you' first for emphasis: to you, and not to someone else. The KJV's 'will I pray' is acceptable; the Hebrew form is a habitual imperfect, 'I am praying' as a settled practice. Notice that the KJV 'Hearken unto the voice' has aged badly; 'voice' (qol) here is the sheer sound of the cry.

philological_notes.note: A cry for help, shouted for rescue; Malbim defines it as the cry of one who calls for salvation.
Causative: 'make your ear attentive', 'pay attention'. Radak notes the verb takes ל, אל or ב.

verses.translation_literal: YHWH, morning you hear my voice; morning I lay out [my prayer] for you, and I keep watch.
verses.translation_dramatic: O LORD, with the morning you hear my voice. With the morning I set my words in order before you, and then I wait, eyes watching, for what you will do.
verses.directors_commentary:
Two clauses, one word repeated: "morning ... morning". Play the repetition as a ritual, a daily habit. The morning is the hour before the day's business begins (Radak, Metzudat David) and, for Rashi, the hour at which God judges the wicked, as in Psalm 101:8 and Isaiah 33:2. The speaker begins the day by coming to the king before anyone else does.

The verb is the one to notice. עָרַךְ is "arrange, set in order, lay out in rows": it is used for the wood laid on an altar, a battle line drawn up, a table set. The Hebrew gives no object. The tradition supplies one: "my prayer" (Rashi, Ibn Ezra, Radak, Metzudat David), and Ibn Ezra calls it an omission, as if the text said "I lay out my prayer for you". The KJV's "direct my prayer" supplies the same object, so it is not an invention. What it loses is the arranging, ordering sense: the prayer is not aimed like an arrow, it is set out in order, like the altar or the table. The same verb is also used of laying out a case before a judge (Job 13:18), a sense that fits the courtroom morning of Rashi's reading, but it is only an overtone here, not the primary meaning.

The last verb, וַאֲצַפֶּה, is "and I keep watch", the posture of a sentry on a wall looking out for what is coming (Radak: "I wait for you to grant my request"). The KJV's "look up" turns the watchman's stance into a pious gesture of the eyes. Here the watching is outward, toward what God will do.

philological_notes.note: 'I arrange, set in order'; used for altar wood, battle lines and laid-out cases. No object is stated; Rashi, Ibn Ezra, Radak and Metzudat David supply 'my prayer'. Rashi, after Menahem, links it to maarakhah, an ordered array. The legal-case sense (Job 13:18) is a possible overtone.

'And I keep watch', the verb for a lookout (tzofeh). Radak glosses it as 'I wait for you to give my request'; Metzudat Zion as 'I hope'. Rashi, on his judgment reading, takes it as 'that you will execute judgments on them'.

verses.translation_literal: For not a God desiring wickedness [are] you; evil does not sojourn with you.
verses.translation_dramatic: For you are no God who delights in wickedness. Evil finds no lodging with you.
verses.directors_commentary: Here the psalm turns from asking to arguing, and its premise needs the ancient setting to be felt. The neighbours of Israel worshipped gods who were themselves capricious, violent and lustful, so a worshipper could never be sure that a god did not take pleasure in cruelty; Malbim makes this point at length, contrasting the pagan pantheon with the God of Israel, who is the source of good alone. The speaker says: I can rely on your justice, because you are not like that. The word garu, 'sojourn', is the language of the resident alien, the ger, who lives under another's roof and protection. Evil, in other words, cannot even be a guest in God's house. The KJV's 'neither shall evil dwell with thee' keeps the sense well, and 'hath pleasure in' is an acceptable rendering of hafetz; but the Hebrew word order puts 'not' before 'a God', a very pointed phrase: not a god of this sort at all.

philological_notes.note: 'Sojourn with you, stay as a guest in your house'; Rashi and Radak read it as 'dwell with you', and Radak compares Job 31:18.
'Taking delight in, wanting'. 'Pleasure' in the KJV is correct but the sense is stronger: desiring.

verses.translation_literal: Boasters will not take their stand before your eyes; you hate all workers of wickedness.
verses.translation_dramatic: The swaggering cannot hold their ground under your gaze. You hate every one who does wrong.
verses.directors_commentary: The image is of a royal audience. Subjects stood before a king, and Ibn Ezra observes that yityatzvu is the word for servants standing in attendance on their lord. The holelim are those who make themselves loud: the root is the same as hallel, 'to praise', turned inward, so these are people who praise themselves, boast or rave. Rashi glosses them as madmen, and Radak notes that the word moves between 'foolish' and 'wicked'. The KJV's 'the foolish' is the weaker end of that range; the Hebrew sense is the self-trumpeting, reckless type. The most striking phrase is 'before your eyes' (leneged einekha): they cannot bear to be looked at. Radak compares it to a man who hates someone and cannot stand to look him in the face. 'Workers of wickedness' (po'alei aven) is the standard phrase for those who make trouble; aven is not just sin but also the trouble it causes (Metzudat Zion: toil and falsehood). The KJV's 'iniquity' is fine as a word, though dead as a sound.

philological_notes.note: Boasters, braggarts, the unhinged; Rashi 'madmen', Radak and Metzudat Zion 'fools'. The same root gives hallel 'praise'.
Wickedness as trouble and falsehood; Metzudat Zion gives 'toil and falsehood'.

verses.translation_literal: You destroy speakers of falsehood; a man of bloods and deceit YHWH abhors.
verses.translation_dramatic: You wipe out those who speak lies. The man of blood and fraud, the LORD finds him loathsome.
verses.directors_commentary: Two verbs of divine reaction, 'destroy' and 'abhor', frame two kinds of person, and the second phrase is the surprise: 'a man of bloods and deceit'. Damim is plural, 'bloods', the ordinary Hebrew word for bloodshed or murder; the KJV's 'bloody' makes it an adjective and softens the point that this is a man who kills. The pairing of killing with deceit is not accidental. In the speaker's world the common way to harm a man was to lie about him to the authorities, and Metzudat David reads the verse exactly so: the slanderer who spoke against David before Saul, hiding murder behind friendly words. The verb yeta'ev, 'abhors', is the strong word, to'evah, used for what is ritually and morally revolting. Note the KJV's 'leasing' for kazav: a word from Old English meaning lying, which no modern reader recognizes. The Hebrew switches from 'you' to the third person, naming YHWH at the end, and Radak points out that this is a normal shift of address.

philological_notes.note: Literally 'a man of bloods', a murderer or bloodthirsty man. The plural is the usual Hebrew for shed blood.
'Abhors, finds loathsome'; Ibn Ezra reads 'he is loathsome and repugnant in His eyes'.

verses.translation_literal: But I, in the greatness of your covenant loyalty, will enter your house; I will bow down toward your holy temple in awe of you.
verses.translation_dramatic: But I, by the sheer size of your faithful love, will walk into your house. I will bow low toward your holy temple, with fear of you in me.
verses.directors_commentary: The emphatic 'And I' (va'ani) swings the scene from the enemy to the speaker, and the contrast is deliberate: they cannot stand before your eyes, but I may come in. And the reason is not his merit. It is rov hasdekha, the abundance of your covenant loyalty (hesed), the word for the undeserved, binding faithfulness of God to his people; Meiri says explicitly that this is despite the speaker being unworthy. The KJV's 'mercy' is too soft; hesed includes loyalty and obligation. Two details of movement matter. 'I will enter your house': this is a visit to a sanctuary, and Radak identifies the 'house' with the place where the ark stood. 'Toward your holy temple' (el heikhal kodshekha): you bow in the direction of the holy place. Heikhal is also a word for a palace, so the temple is God's royal hall. And the final phrase, 'in awe of you', is not trembling fear of punishment; Ibn Ezra reads it as the speaker's only offering, because he has nothing else to bring.

philological_notes.note: Covenant loyalty, steadfast love; more than 'mercy'. The speaker enters God's house because of it, not because of his own worth (Meiri).
Heikhal means both 'palace' and 'temple'; 'your holy palace-temple'. Radak identifies the house as the sanctuary housing the ark.
'In awe of you'; reverence, not terror. Ibn Ezra: the speaker brings no offering but his awe.

verses.translation_literal: YHWH, lead me in your righteousness because of my watchers; make straight before me your way.
verses.translation_dramatic: LORD, guide me by your justice. Look how they watch me. Make your road straight in front of my face.
verses.directors_commentary: The hinge of the psalm: after the contrast between God and the wicked, the speaker states his actual need. He is surrounded by people who are watching him, waiting for his foot to slip. The Hebrew word is shorerai, from the root shur, 'to look at, to lie in wait', the verb of Balaam's 'I see him, but not near' (Numbers 24:17); Rashi, Radak and Ibn Ezra all draw that connection. The KJV's 'mine enemies' is accurate in spirit but loses the picture: these are enemies who are watching, hoping for him to fall. The petition is double: lead me, and make the way straight. Malbim distinguishes the two: the first is about not losing the road, the second about clearing obstacles in advance, before I set my foot there. A 'straight way' before the face is a prepared road, with no pits. The Qere hayshar differs in spelling from the Ketiv, which Radak also records. Note that 'righteousness' (tzidkah) here is God's own, by which he leads, not the speaker's.

philological_notes.note: Those who watch me, lie in wait for me; Rashi and Radak connect it with Numbers 24:17. Close to 'enemies' but with the watching image intact.
Qere: 'make straight' (a causative imperative). The written form is הושר. Radak discusses the spelling.

verses.translation_literal: For there is not in his mouth [anything] reliable; their inner being is ruin; an open grave [is] their throat; their tongue they make smooth.
verses.translation_dramatic: For not one word from his mouth can be trusted. Inside they are ruin. Their throat is an open grave, and their tongue they make smooth as oil.
verses.directors_commentary: The portrait of the enemies is built from body parts: mouth, inner organs, throat, tongue. Each is a stage on a descent. The words are slippery (the tongue is 'made smooth'), the throat is a grave gaping for its victim, and deep inside, where nobody sees, there is havot, ruin. Rashi reads the point as friendship worn as a mask: they look like friends and are enemies; Metzudat David sees the same: they appear to love and are in fact hunting. The image of the 'open grave' is the most vivid in the psalm, and the KJV's 'open sepulchre' is correct but now sounds Gothic. The idea is of a mouth that swallows. It is the same picture as Sheol with its mouth wide: whoever walks into the slick speech slides down the throat into the pit (Malbim develops this). The KJV's 'their inward part is very wickedness' is loose; havot is 'ruin, destruction' (Metzudat Zion and Meiri), not wickedness. The singular 'his mouth' beside plural 'their' is Hebrew distributing the phrase over each individual: in no one's mouth.

philological_notes.note: Ruin, calamity (Metzudat Zion, Meiri). Rashi reads 'deceit'. The KJV 'very wickedness' obscures this.
'They make smooth, they flatter'; smooth words that slide past suspicion. Ibn Ezra links it with 'smooth' (halak).
Something firm, reliable. Radak supplies 'a word' as the missing noun.

verses.translation_literal: Hold them guilty, O God; may they fall from their own counsels; for the multitude of their transgressions banish them, for they have rebelled against you.
verses.translation_dramatic: Declare them guilty, God. Let them fall by their own schemes. For all their crimes, drive them out, because they rose in revolt against you.
verses.directors_commentary: This is the verse that readers skip because it sounds harsh, and here the English tradition does the most smoothing. The first verb, ha'ashimem, is from asham, 'guilt': it is a legal command, 'declare them guilty', 'hold them liable' (ASV and YLT have it right). The KJV and Webster's 'Destroy thou them' blunts a courtroom request into a curse. The speaker asks for a verdict, not for revenge. The second request is poetic justice: let them fall from, or through, their own plans (mo'atzot, counsels); Ibn Ezra puts it simply: their own counsel will make them fall. Hadichemo, 'banish them', is the word for being driven out, thrust away from a place. The final clause, maru vakh, 'they rebelled against you', changes the whole picture: the enemies are not just David's enemies; they are rebels against God, and it is the rebellion, not the injury to the speaker, that justifies the prayer. Radak ties this to the enemies who rejected the king God appointed. The speaker is a king asking the heavenly king to enforce a verdict.

philological_notes.note: Causative of 'be guilty': 'declare guilty, hold liable'. Radak also notes the reading from 'desolate'. KJV 'destroy' loses the legal sense.
'They rebelled, they defied'; Metzudat Zion links it with meri, rebellion.
'Drive them away, thrust them out'; the form with -mo is poetic.

verses.translation_literal: And let all who seek refuge in you rejoice; for ever let them shout for joy, and you may cover over them; and let those who love your name exult in you.
verses.translation_dramatic: But let everyone who takes refuge in you rejoice. Let them sing out forever, while you spread your cover over them. And let all who love your name leap for joy in you.
verses.directors_commentary: The psalm ends in a crowd scene, and the dramatic turn is the contrast with the previous verse: those who rebelled are driven out, those who took refuge are brought in. The verb chosen, chasah, 'to seek refuge', is the word for a creature running under shelter, and the verb that follows, taSekh, 'you cover', comes from the root for a booth or thicket: God is the booth over their heads. Rashi glosses it as 'protect and shelter', and Radak as a covering that keeps the enemies from harming them. The KJV 'because thou defendest them' turns the shelter into a military defence. The three verbs of joy are distinct: yismechu (be glad), yeranenu (ring out, shout aloud) and ya'letzu (exult, leap), which Metzudat Zion simply glosses 'be glad'. The speaker's own private prayer in the morning has widened to a chorus of all those who love 'your name', for in Israel the name stood for God's whole presence. Malbim notes that the joy should be lasting, not only after the trouble has passed.

philological_notes.note: Those who take refuge, as under a shelter. Radak sets them against the enemies who do not trust in God.
'You may cover over', as a booth (sukkah) covers; Rashi 'protect and shelter', Radak 'be a covering over them'. Ibn Ezra notes the missing dagesh.
To exult, to leap with joy; Metzudat Zion glosses simply 'be glad'.

verses.translation_literal: For you, you bless [the] righteous, YHWH; like a large shield, favor, you surround him.
verses.translation_dramatic: For it is you, LORD, who blesses the one who is in the right. Like a great shield raised before a man and curved about him, so your favor closes round him on every side.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the verse's grounding clause: the "for" (ki) explains why those who love God's name can sing at the end of verse 12. The speaker has spent the psalm among liars, bloodthirsty men and open graves for throats (v. 10). Now the voice drops from plea to certainty, and the actor should let it settle rather than shout it. The word "righteous" (tzaddiq) is not a title of moral perfection but a legal one: the person who is in the right in a dispute, the one a court would acquit. The speaker has been pleading his case before God at dawn (v. 4), and this is the verdict he expects.

The KJV's "wilt compass him" is the archaic sense of "compass" as "encircle," now almost lost, and its "with favour... as with a shield" reverses the Hebrew order and smooths away the point. The Hebrew puts the shield first and the favor second: "like a shield, favor, you surround him." Favor (ratzon) is the thing that does the shielding. YLT's "buckler" suggests too small a thing. A tzinnah is the large body shield carried before an infantryman, tall enough that he could crouch behind it. Rashi and Meiri both say it wraps a man on three sides, and Rashi's gloss on ratzon is "contentment, peace of mind." So the image is of a soldier who is not merely covered but calm. Note too the echo of verse 12: God "spreads a cover" (tasekh) over the refugees, here he "surrounds" them, both pictures of a protection that is pitched around the person like a tent wall.

philological_notes.note: A large body shield, distinct from the smaller magen ("buckler"), as in Goliath's shield-bearer in 1 Sam 17:7. The KJV's single word "shield" does not distinguish them. Rashi and Meiri explain it as the shield that surrounds a person on three sides, which is why "surround" is the natural verb here.

Favor, goodwill, the pleasure of someone in power toward his subject. Rashi glosses it as "contentment" (nachat ruach), Meiri as "reconciliation, ease of mind." The shield is made of God's goodwill, not of anything the righteous man holds himself.

"You surround him." The root is the same as the "crown" (atarah), a thing that goes all the way round the head. Rashi, Radak and Metzudat Zion take it as "encircle," citing 1 Sam 23:26, where Saul's men "were surrounding" David. Ibn Ezra prefers a stem with two objects, "crown him with favor," which keeps the word's crown sense.
